title: Washington Ethics Advisory Opinion 26-02
text:
Opinion 26-02
Questions:
My niece, who lives locally here in same county as me, has recently become engaged. I have known this person (her fiancé) for a number of years (approximately 4-5). They became engaged this past spring. They do not live together nor do they share finances. He recently entered the police academy and is now an officer in my town. We are a small jurisdiction. We have three Superior Court Judges and two District Court judges. We rotate on-call once every five weeks, which means all calls during non-business hours for search warrants, etc. are handled by the on-call judge for both Superior and District Court cases.
How this plays out is often the court will have to determine probable cause for a case to set release conditions, search warrants, etc. Additionally, if there are motion hearings or trials, the court will have to make decisions. I am going to assume he (the fiancé) will be calling me when I am on-call for search warrants, as well as submitting reports upon arrest of individuals, where I will need to consider probable cause. As he is a brand-new officer, this has not happened yet, but it is anticipated.
How does this impact me ethically now that my niece is engaged to a law enforcement officer? I see my niece multiple times a month. I see her fiancé less often, usually for holidays, birthdays, family dinners, etc. We have made it a point since he became an officer here locally that we don't attend the same family functions, such as Thanksgiving, birthdays, dinners, exchange gifts, etc.
If any of these situations present a conflict requiring recusal, can the parties waive my recusal?
Answer:
CJC Rule 2.11(A)(2)(d) states that if a person within a third degree of relationship to a judicial officer or the judicial officer's spouse, or such person's spouse or domestic partner, is likely to be a material witness, the judicial officer shall self-disqualify from the case. Third degree of relationship includes nieces and nephews. CJC Terminology.
Because a law enforcement officer who is engaged to the judicial officer's niece is not within a third degree of relationship to the judicial officer, self-disqualification is not necessarily required. However, if the fiancé of the judicial officer's niece is signing probable cause affidavits, search warrant affidavits, or may otherwise be a material witness in such cases, then the judicial officer should consider whether disclosure of the relationship is required. CJC Rule 2.11 Comment [5]. Also, after the law enforcement officer marries the judicial officer's niece, disqualification would be required where the law enforcement officer may be a material witness because the law enforcement officer is then the spouse of someone within a third degree of relationship to the judicial officer. CJC Rule 2.11(A)(2)(d).
In EAO 94-01, a judge's spouse worked as a supervisor in the sheriff's office. This Committee said the judicial officer should disclose any circumstance that might cause the judicial officer's impartiality to reasonably be questioned. Such circumstances could include the spouse's employment with the sheriff's office, and whether officers involved in a case are supervised by the spouse. This Committee concluded the judge should not hear cases involving officers supervised by the judge's spouse; should not sign warrants for officers supervised by the judge's spouse; and for other warrants, should ask questions to make sure officers supervised by the spouse were not involved in the case.
Similarly, EAO 17-04 involved a spouse employed by the sheriff's office that was not on patrol assignment, did not make stops or arrests, did not conduct investigations, and did not supervise other officers. The Committee concluded recusal was not required, but disclosure of the relationship was necessary in any cases involving the sheriff's office because parties or their lawyers might reasonably consider the spouse's employment relevant to a possible motion to disqualify.
Although the question presented does not automatically lead to disqualification at this time, parties or their lawyers could find the relationship relevant to a motion to disqualify on the basis that the judicial officer's impartiality might reasonably be questioned. Therefore, the judicial officer should disclose the relationship on the record. CJC Rule 2.11 Comment [5].
